copious

/KOH-pee-us/ — three syllables: CO-pi-ous · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Copious describes something that exists in large, plentiful amounts, more than enough.

She took copious notes, filling two notebooks in a single lecture.

Example

She took copious notes throughout the semester, filling three thick folders with detailed observations and cross-references.

Copious captures the overflowing abundance of notes—not just many pages, but an outpouring and profusion. It is more precise than "many" or "lots of" because it conveys the sheer volume and sense of things flowing forth in great supply.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

plentiful: Plentiful says a supply is large and easy to draw on — plentiful firewood, plentiful daylight. It stops at how much is available. Copious describes what someone produces or gathers in generous, more-than-needed amounts: copious notes, copious tears. Plentiful measures what is available; copious measures what pours out.

profuse: Profuse describes something gushing out beyond control — profuse apologies, profuse sweat — a flow that feels involuntary. Copious is calmer and often deliberate: a generously large amount produced on purpose, like notes that cover everything. Profuse suggests an uncontrolled flow; copious suggests planned plenty.

voluminous: Voluminous is a claim about physical bulk — voluminous files fill a drawer, a voluminous coat fills a doorway. It measures the space something takes up. Copious measures amount against need: more than enough. Notes can be copious in content while still fitting into one slim notebook.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sparse: thinly spread, with little present

scanty: barely enough to count as sufficient

Where it sits · how much more than needed there is

meager → moderate → copious → overflowing

meager vs. copious: Meager is the opposite of copious: meager notes are thin and barely enough, while copious notes fill page after page.

moderate vs. copious: Moderate sits in the middle, well below copious — a moderate amount is reasonable and measured, while a copious amount is generously more than required.

overflowing vs. copious: Overflowing pushes past even copious: copious describes a generously large amount produced, while overflowing means it can no longer be contained at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — copi: plenty, an ample supply (Latin copia) (Latin)

Suffix — -ous: full of (Latin)

Put it together: The root copia means 'plenty, an ample supply' (itself built long ago from co- 'together' + ops 'wealth'), and -ous means 'full of' — so copious literally means 'full of plenty,' describing amounts produced or recorded in generous supply.

Use the root in a new word: cornucopia: Grandma set the cornucopia at the center of the Thanksgiving table before the guests arrived.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Copious is the word when you want to emphasize an outpouring or profusion—abundance that seems to flow forth generously. For everyday quantities, 'plenty' or 'plentiful' is simpler and clear.
